items.prompt: What is a bounded context, as this unit defines it?
choices: A database table shared by two teams
The boundary around a part of a system where a concept's specific meaning and rules hold
A microservice's network boundary
A team's org-chart reporting line
items.explanation: A bounded context is defined by where a concept's meaning and guarantees hold — the same word can mean something different just outside that boundary.
items.reference:
Bounded context
boundary around a specific meaning
same word can mean something else outside it

Why: The boundary is about meaning and guarantees, not about physical or network structure.

items.prompt: Why can Sales' 'Order' and Warehouse's 'Order' be considered two different concepts even though both teams use the same word?
choices: Because the teams disagree about the dictionary definition of 'order'
Because each 'Order' carries different guarantees within its own bounded context, even with the same one-sentence definition
Because Sales and Warehouse use different programming languages
Because Warehouse's team is smaller than Sales' team
items.explanation: Both teams would give the same plain-English definition, but the guarantees each context's Order carries — safe to ship or not — genuinely differ.
items.reference:
Bounded context
boundary around a specific meaning
same word can mean something else outside it

Why: The boundary is about meaning and guarantees, not about physical or network structure.

items.prompt: What is a context map?
choices: A network diagram showing which services call which APIs
A picture of which bounded contexts exist and how they relate to and depend on each other
A list of every database table in a system
An org chart of which teams own which services
items.explanation: A context map is specifically about bounded contexts and their relationships — not a generic architecture or org diagram.
items.reference:
Context map
which bounded contexts exist
how they relate/depend on each other

Why: A context map tracks meaning boundaries, which don't always line up with service or network boundaries. A service is one running part of a software system, such as checkout or shipping.

items.prompt: Why is a context map different from a typical service architecture diagram?
choices: They're the same thing, just with different names
A context map tracks where meaning changes, which can happen inside a single service or span multiple services sharing one meaning
A context map only applies to microservices, never to monoliths
A context map shows server locations and network latency
items.explanation: Two services can share one bounded context, and a single service can straddle two bounded contexts — the map follows meaning, not network topology.
items.reference:

how they relate/depend on each other

Why: A context map tracks meaning boundaries, which don't always line up with service or network boundaries. A service is one running part of a software system, such as checkout or shipping.

items.prompt: If two services always agree on what every term means and share identical guarantees, how would they typically be treated on a context map?
choices: As one bounded context spanning both services, not two separate ones
As two bounded contexts, because they're separate services
As two bounded contexts, but only if owned by different teams
As two bounded contexts, but only if they use different databases
items.explanation: Bounded contexts are defined by meaning and guarantees, not by service boundaries — services that fully agree on both can be treated as one context.
items.reference:
Context map

items.prompt: In an upstream/downstream relationship between two bounded contexts, who has to adapt when the other one changes?
choices: The upstream context adapts to the downstream context
The downstream context adapts to changes in the upstream context
Neither adapts — they change independently with no effect on each other
Both contexts must always change together
items.explanation: The upstream context's model evolves on its own schedule; the downstream context is the one that has to adapt when it changes.
items.reference:
Upstream / downstream
upstream changes on its own schedule
downstream adapts to it

Why: It's a relationship, not a symmetric partnership — one side sets the pace.

items.prompt: In the Sales/Warehouse example, which context is upstream?
choices: Warehouse, because it ships the physical goods
Sales, because its Order model changes independently and Warehouse has to adapt to it
Neither — they're peers with equal influence over each other's models
It depends on which team has more engineers
items.explanation: Sales is upstream — its model evolves on its own schedule, and Warehouse's anticorruption layer is what absorbs those changes.
items.reference:
Upstream / downstream
upstream changes on its own schedule
downstream adapts to it

Why: It's a relationship, not a symmetric partnership — one side sets the pace.

items.prompt: What is an anticorruption layer?
choices: A security firewall between two networks
A deliberate translation step at the boundary between two contexts, so one context's internal model never leaks directly into another's
A code review process for catching bugs before deployment
A shared database table both teams write to
items.explanation: The anticorruption layer's job is translation at the boundary — it's what Sales and Warehouse were missing before the fix.
items.reference:
Anticorruption layer
translates at the boundary
keeps each context's own model clean

Why: Without it, one team's internal model becomes a silent dependency for another team's system.

items.prompt: Why did Warehouse need an anticorruption layer instead of just fixing Sales' Order model directly?
choices: Because Sales' team refused to make any changes at all
Because Sales genuinely needs an Order that exists before payment clears, for its own use cases like cart pages and abandoned-cart emails
Because anticorruption layers are always required by convention
Because Warehouse's database couldn't store Sales' data format
items.explanation: Forcing Sales' model to already mean 'safe to ship' would break Sales' own legitimate use cases — the translation belongs at the boundary, not inside Sales' model.
items.reference:
Anticorruption layer
translates at the boundary
keeps each context's own model clean

Why: Without it, one team's internal model becomes a silent dependency for another team's system.

items.prompt: Sales and Warehouse both define 'Order' the same way in conversation. Why did their systems still break when wired together directly?
choices: Because their definitions were actually different, they just didn't realize it
Because the same word carried different guarantees in each team's system, even with a matching plain-language definition
Because Warehouse's engineers made a typo in their code
Because Sales' database was slower than Warehouse's
items.explanation: The mismatch wasn't in the definition — it was in what each context silently assumed was already true whenever the word was used.
items.reference:
Same word, different guarantees
Sales' Order: exists before payment/stock confirmed
Warehouse's Order: must be safe to ship

Why: Agreement on a word's definition doesn't guarantee agreement on what's silently assumed true whenever it's used.

items.prompt: What specifically made Sales' 'Order' unsafe for Warehouse to act on immediately?

Sales' Order was stored in a different file format
Sales' Order didn't include a customer name
Sales' Order was created by a different programming team

items.reference:
Same word, different guarantees
Sales' Order: exists before payment/stock confirmed
Warehouse's Order: must be safe to ship

Why: Agreement on a word's definition doesn't guarantee agreement on what's silently assumed true whenever it's used.

items.prompt: What is a shared kernel, as one of the integration patterns between bounded contexts?
choices: A small, jointly-owned piece of the model that both contexts deliberately share and agree to change together
A single database used by every team in the company
A pattern where one context copies another's code without asking
A rule that only one team may ever touch a codebase
items.explanation: A shared kernel works when two teams are willing to coordinate tightly on a small, jointly-owned piece of the model and change it together.
items.reference:
Integration patterns
Anticorruption layertranslate at boundary
Conformistadopt upstream as-is
Shared kerneljointly-owned shared piece

Example: Sales and Warehouse might jointly own a tiny PaymentConfirmed event and agree to change it together.

Why: Each pattern trades off coordination cost against how much each side controls its own model.

items.explanation: Unlike an anticorruption layer (which keeps each context's model independent), a shared kernel means both teams agree to jointly own and evolve one piece together.
items.reference:
Integration patterns

each context's model stays true to its own needs
